narrative:
The promotion decision was based on a model estimate that you have a 79% chance of leaving your job in the near future. In practical terms, the organization is treating your retention risk as high, so it is holding back the promotion rather than investing in a role move it believes you may soon exit.

The strongest signal behind that prediction is your overall experience level. With six to ten years of total experience, you sit outside the largest group of predicted stayers, who most often have only one to five years; this raises the estimated risk that you may be mobile. The second strongest signal is that you have received other job opportunities while in this job. Only about one in four predicted stayers reported that, so outside options are treated as a meaningful pull toward leaving. Third, your one-to-five years in the current organization is common among stayers, but together with your broader experience it still adds to the leaving risk rather than offsetting it.

Your profile also includes mixed signals: you are very satisfied overall and feel recognized, but you reported no deserved promotion, no income-for-effort satisfaction, difficult work-life balance, psychological exhaustion, frequent business travel, and medium job support. These contextual pressures make retention risk more plausible.

Before reconsidering promotion, discuss concrete retention steps: clarify a promotion path and timing, review pay and rewards relative to effort, address workload and travel, and test whether outside opportunities are the main driver.
